newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia seen becoming post-EMU "safe haven".
newsitem.headline: Australia seen becoming post-EMU "safe haven".

text.p: Australian financial assets could become more attractive with the launch of the European single currency in 1999 as investors seek to diversify and perhaps seek a safe haven in the early days of uncertainty, analysts say.
Major corporate lenders could have most to gain if offshore investors gobble up limited supplies of Australian government bonds and pour funds into local corporate debt.
"Global asset managers will seek to diversify out of the euro," said Michael Ullmer, chairman of Coopers & Lybrand's financial services group.
Ullmer told a seminar last week that monetary union, set for January 1999, would result in a deeper, more liquid market and exchange rate convergence would result in reduced volatility.
This would present opportunities for Australia as well as the rest of the Asia-Pacific region, he said.
Glenn Maguire, senior economist with Societe Generale, told the same seminar that monetary union would create one of the largest government bond markets in the world.
"The euro benchmarks will have an increased importance on Australian bonds," Maguire said.

"Real rates of return on Australian dollar-denominated debt will remain higher than euro-denominated debt," he said, although Australian debt would only account for around one percent of global bond markets.
"Australia will stand out as a high real yielder."

However, Maguire said the EMU could present some risks for the Australian dollar against the euro, particularly if the new European Central Bank did not properly dispose of its large holdings of U.S. dollars.
The AUD-euro exchange rate will largely be determined by the U.S. dollar-euro cross rate.
Maguire noted the European Central Bank would hold large quantities of U.S. dollars for intervention purposes.
"This amount may no longer be appropriate, prompting the European Central Bank to sell excess U.S. dollars," he said,
"The Australian dollar could be dragged down against the euro if the USD overhang is not managed properly."
However, he said the U.S. dollar was likely to strengthen initially against the untested euro.

"Like the U.S. dollar, Australia could well benefit as a 'safe haven'," Maguire said. "There will be continuing bouts of uncertainty about the sustainability of the euro after 1 January, 1999," he said.

Wayne Hoy, chief manager financial markets at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, told Reuters that international investors and central banks would "rediversify" risk into currencies such as the Australian dollar and the Canadian dollar.
Hoy said international interest in Australian government securities would increase, creating an increased overall pressure on Australian bonds.
This situation would be positive for Australia as official debt would be in tight supply and Australian investors would turn to corporate debt, he said.
"Ultimately Australian corporates will get the advantage." he said.
